SERVICES.cra:
Credit reference agencies: i Banks and other lenders usually report a name change to credit reference agencies eventually, but this happens passively and can take a while, and does not always link your old and new name cleanly.

For a faster, more reliable option, contact Experian, Equifax, or TransUnion directly and ask for their gender transition or name change guide. The three UK agencies have an agreement to notify each other on your behalf, with your consent, but this only starts the process at the other two; it does not complete it. Each agency still has its own separate form, and you will usually need to send your own ID and proof of address to each one before your file there is updated.

⚠️ Notice of Correction: Adding a Notice of Correction can help explain a split or mismatched credit history, but it also means lenders have to manually review any application you make rather than using automated decision-making, which can slow down applications for credit while it's in place.

⚠️ Privacy note: An unmerged file can show your old name to a landlord, lender, or letting agent running a credit check on you. Check back after a few weeks to confirm the merge has gone through, and follow up directly with any agency that has not been in touch.

dvla.variants.both:
The DVLA handles driving licence updates. i Your gender marker is stored in the number on your licence and should update as part of the process. You can also use the title Mx on your driving licence. You will also need a separate document that already shows your new name.

Driving licence updates for name or gender are handled by post. The DVLA website linked below has the full details, including what to send and the application form.

⚠️ Evidence needed: As well as your deed poll or statutory declaration, the DVLA asks for one other document that already shows your new name. It must be dated after your deed poll or statutory declaration, and after your current licence if you already hold one.

Issued in the last 12 months:

  • A letter from HMRC, an employer, or a government department or council
  • A utility bill, including a mobile, broadband, or streaming bill
  • A UK bank statement
  • A voter card
  • A visa or residence permit

With no time limit, as long as it was issued after your deed poll or statutory declaration:

  • A non-UK passport
  • A non-GB driving licence
  • A national identity card

i Your current driving licence cannot be used as this document, since it still shows your old name. It is often quicker to get a mobile, broadband, or streaming bill changed to your new name first, or ask your employer for a letter, rather than wait on a bank statement or a voter card, both of which need you to already be set up under your new name with that organisation.

Gender marker evidence: The DVLA accepts a deed poll or a statutory declaration for a combined name and gender change. If you would rather use a GRC, it must be sent together with a deed poll or a statutory declaration, since a GRC on its own is not accepted for a combined change.

Cost note: Updating your name and gender marker is usually free. A photo update at the same time may carry a small fee. Check GOV.UK for prices.

⚠️ Legal requirement: Updating your gender marker is optional, but telling the DVLA about a name change is not as you can face a large fine for not doing so.

grc_docs:
Paperwork for your GRC application As well as the medical reports and the two years of evidence, the application asks for a statutory declaration, your full birth or adoption certificate, and copies of anything showing a change of name.

These are the documents the application asks for besides the medical reports and the evidence of living in your affirmed gender. You can usually send copies, but keep the originals, as the panel may ask to see them after you apply.

Statutory declaration: GOV.UK provides the declaration itself, along with guidance on which version applies to you and who can witness your signature.

Birth or adoption certificate: an original or certified copy of the full certificate. If your birth or adoption was registered in the UK and you do not have it to hand, you can order a copy.

Name-change documents: if you have changed your name, you need copies of everything showing when you did so. This includes both enrolled and unenrolled deed polls, and statutory declarations of a name change. These copies do not need to be certified.

If you have ever been married or in a civil partnership: you also need copies of every marriage or civil partnership certificate. If you are currently in one and intend to stay in it, your spouse or civil partner completes a statutory declaration of their own. If a marriage or civil partnership has ended, you need the decree absolute, final order, or your partner's death certificate instead.

If any document is not in English: it needs a translation. The translator does not need any qualifications, so a friend or family member can do it, and you send both the original and the translation.

grc_med.regions.default:
Medical proof for GRC A GRC is the UK's legal route to having your gender legally recognised. It only ever recognises you as male or female; GOV.UK states plainly that non-binary genders are not legally recognised in the UK. The application also requires two medical reports; the GOV.UK links below have details on what is needed.

The GRC application requires two medical reports. Both must be written by either two different medical doctors registered in the UK, or a medical doctor and a clinical psychologist, both registered in the UK. A nurse practitioner cannot write either report.

The first report must come from a registered doctor or clinical psychologist who practises in the field of gender dysphoria. GOV.UK publishes a list of specialists, but says this list is not complete and not always up to date; someone not on the list can still write this report if they include a brief summary of their experience in the field.

The second report can come from any registered doctor or clinical psychologist, including a GP, a surgeon, or an endocrinologist. There is no set content for this second report. Reports do not need to be written specially for your application if you already have ones that meet these requirements.

If your gender has already been legally changed in another country, the UK may accept that instead. The GOV.UK links below have the application requirements, the list of specialists, and the list of recognised countries.

UK Gender Recognition Certificate (GRC) A GRC is the UK's legal route to having your gender recognised, updating your birth certificate, marriage records, HMRC, and pensions. It only ever recognises you as male or female; GOV.UK states plainly that non-binary genders are not legally recognised in the UK. The application also requires two medical reports; the GOV.UK links below have details on what is needed.

The UK Gender Recognition Act 2004 is the standard route for legal gender recognition across the UK.

A UK GRC still has practical uses in Northern Ireland for birth certificate, marriage and civil partnership records, HMRC, DfC/DWP, and pensions.

The application requires two medical reports. Both must be written by either two different medical doctors registered in the UK, or a medical doctor and a clinical psychologist, both registered in the UK. A nurse practitioner cannot write either report.

The first report must come from a registered doctor or clinical psychologist who practises in the field of gender dysphoria. GOV.UK publishes a list of specialists, but says this list is not complete and not always up to date; someone not on the list can still write this report if they include a brief summary of their experience in the field.

The second report can come from any registered doctor or clinical psychologist, including a GP, a surgeon, or an endocrinologist. There is no set content for this second report. Reports do not need to be written specially for your application if you already have ones that meet these requirements.

If your gender has already been legally changed in another country, the UK may accept that instead. The GOV.UK links below have the application requirements, the list of specialists, and the list of recognised countries.

Update your records with HMRC. You can ask them to protect your records so fewer people can see them. Your tax records, payslips, and benefits payments will then use the correct name and details.

Name changes: HMRC can update your name when notified. You can also ask them to restrict access to your records for privacy — see the note below on how this works without a Gender Recognition Certificate. The HMRC team that handles this is called "Special Section D", and restricted records are looked after by "Public Department 1" (PD1). Knowing these names can help if you need to chase things up by phone. The GOV.UK link below has the details.

⚠️ If you are 16 or 17: Your National Insurance number is usually sent automatically shortly before your 16th birthday, based on your Child Benefit record, so the letter may arrive in your old name. The number itself never changes and does not need updating, but you can still tell HMRC your new name the same way as above. The GOV.UK link below has the details.

Gender marker changes: If you have a Gender Recognition Certificate (GRC), HMRC is usually notified automatically and your records are moved to a restricted file; only specialist staff can access them. HMRC has confirmed it does not change the gender marker on a record without a GRC — but restricting your records for privacy is a separate matter from the gender marker itself. i Some people without a GRC report that Special Section D can still apply the same restriction if asked directly, though HMRC holds no published guidance either way, so treat this as worth asking about rather than guaranteed. The GOV.UK link below has the details.

Home country passport The rules for updating your home country passport depend on your country of origin. UKVI usually needs an updated home country passport before a UK eVisa can be changed.

Your first step is usually to check directly with your home country's embassy or consulate in the UK as they can tell you whether a gender marker change is possible and how to apply.

The process and cost varies entirely by country. Some countries do not allow gender marker changes on passports. hr:
Work, payroll, and volunteering Your employer's HR or payroll team can update your records once they have seen your deed poll or statutory declaration.

Sharing your deed poll or statutory declaration with the right team means your payslips, tax reporting, and official records will all use your new name. UK data protection law gives people a right to ask organisations to correct their personal records; the ICO links below explain how this works in an employment context.

For volunteer roles, the person who looks after volunteer records (a coordinator, HR team, or manager) can update things the same way.

Worth flagging to payroll: Ask your payroll team to report a name change and a gender change to HMRC separately as combining them can cause payroll errors, including an inflated tax bill. A gender marker change may also affect your National Insurance category. This does not need action from you, but it can help to point your payroll team at the GOV.UK page below if something looks wrong afterwards.

irish_passport:
Irish passport (Good Friday Agreement route) As someone born in Northern Ireland, you may be able to claim Irish citizenship under the Good Friday Agreement. The Republic of Ireland has a separate process for updating a gender marker on a passport, which differs from the UK GRC route.

Under the Good Friday Agreement, people born in Northern Ireland can claim Irish citizenship. The Republic of Ireland has its own gender recognition process, which works very differently from the UK GRC route. The Department of Foreign Affairs and TENI (Transgender Equality Network Ireland) links below have details on eligibility, requirements, and how to apply.

Evidence needed: If you live in Northern Ireland or anywhere else outside Ireland, the Passport Service asks for a statutory declaration stating that you have a settled and solemn intention of living in your new gender for the rest of your life, together with two documents from two different sources showing use of your new name over at least two years. This applies whether you are applying for your first Irish passport or renewing one. A first application also asks for an identity verification form, your full original birth certificate showing your parents' names, proof of address dated within the last 12 months, and original government-issued photo identification.

⚠️ If you already hold an Irish passport in your previous name: Be aware that applying for an updated passport resets the two-year usage period, which then begins from the issue date of that passport rather than from when you started using your new name.

Note on the Irish GRC: An Irish Gender Recognition Certificate is a separate route. It is only available to people ordinarily resident in the Republic of Ireland, or whose birth, adoption, or foreign birth registration is recorded there, so it does not apply to someone living in Northern Ireland or Great Britain. It is not covered further here. The TENI link below explains the Irish GRC process for people it does apply to.

⚠️ If you are 16 or 17: the published adult guidance does not say whether this route is open to 16 and 17 year olds. If this applies to you, contact the Passport Service before applying to check what you need to do.

When you register at a new HSCNI practice, you can show your deed poll or statutory declaration at registration so your correct details are on file from day one. Ask the practice to use the correct gender marker when registering.

Your GP practice can request a new NHS number with the correct gender marker (for adults), or update your existing record. Your medical care, screening invitations, and correspondence will then use your correct details.

For gender marker updates there are two options. A new NHS number protects your privacy and stops your old name appearing on future letters. Alternatively, your gender marker can be updated on your existing NHS number.

⚠️ Waiting list note: Primary Care Support England (PCSE), which manages this on behalf of NHS England, warns in its own guidance that requesting a new NHS number can mean losing your place on any NHS waiting lists you are on. If you are mid-treatment or mid-referral, weigh this against the privacy benefit of a new number.

⚠️ If you are 16 or 17: Following a 2025 government review, NHS England has stopped issuing new NHS numbers and changing the gender marker on medical records for patients under 18. You can still update your name and title on your GP record at any age. This restriction is specific to NHS England; check with your GP if you are unsure how it applies to you.

⚠️ Screening note: Changing your gender marker may stop automatic NHS screening invitations, for example for cervical or breast screening. Ask your GP to check you are enrolled in the screening programmes right for your body.

Non-binary gender markers: In England, you can ask your GP to record your gender as 'indeterminate' (shown as 'Not specified' in most NHS systems) if you are 18 or over. Ask the practice to use gender code 'I' if they are unsure what to enter.

ukpass:
UK passport

For a name change, your deed poll and evidence of using your new name (such as a bank statement or utility bill) will be needed. For a gender marker change without a GRC, you will also need to write a letter asking for the change of gender, together with a letter from a medical professional (such as your GP or a gender specialist) confirming the change is likely to be permanent. If you already have a GRC, that is accepted as evidence instead of both of these letters.

⚠️ Medical letter: HMPO is strict about what this letter must include. According to HMPO's published guidance, it should:

  • Be written by either a medical professional registered with the General Medical Council (GMC) or the Health and Care Professions Council (HCPC), or a medical professional, in the UK or overseas, who is not registered with either body but who can provide evidence of their qualifications and experience. HMPO gives examples including GPs, gender dysphoria clinicians and specialists, clinical psychologists, consultant psychologists and psychiatrists, practitioner psychologists, and specialist nurses, though this is not a complete list
  • Be dated and include the medical professional's handwritten signature
  • Confirm that the medical professional knows you well enough to make a diagnosis
  • State your name and specified gender
  • Confirm you use your name and gender for all purposes
  • State that your gender change is "likely to be permanent"

If HMPO rejects a letter from a medical professional who is not registered with the GMC or HCPC, it will ask for a new letter from one who is registered. Treat the wider route as a fallback, not the easiest option.

The GOV.UK link below has the full requirements.

⚠️ If you are 16 or 17: unlike a name-only change, a gender marker change usually needs the signed consent of everyone with parental responsibility for you. HMPO can proceed without this in some situations: if you are within two weeks of turning 18, if both your parents have died, or if you have no contact with one or both parents and you explain your circumstances. Where there are safeguarding concerns, none of these apply, and a court order is needed instead. Contact HMPO directly to find out what applies to you.

⚠️ Travel note: Make sure the name on your travel ticket matches your passport. Border Force and airlines may check documents including any eVisa. Mismatches can lead to delays or difficulties when travelling.

⚠️ Non-binary marker: UK passports currently only offer M or F: there is no X or non-binary option. You can still note your identity in the additional information section of your application, but the passport itself will show M or F.
